title: Earthworms and microplastics exert differential effects on the growth, physiology, and root morphological traits of Lolium perenne L. and Medicago sativa L. in a microcosm experiment
content:
Abstract
Soil microplastics have emerged as a potential threat to plant performance, yet how soil fauna regulate plant responses to microplastic stress remains poorly understood. We conducted a 10-week greenhouse microcosm experiment to investigate the individual and interaction effects of earthworms and microplastics on soil properties, root functional traits, photosynthetic performance, and growth of Lolium perenne L. and Medicago sativa L. Compared with L. perenne, M. sativa had higher soil total carbon, organic carbon, and total nitrogen. Microplastic reduced available nitrogen, particularly nitrate nitrogen, whereas earthworms increased soil carbon and nitrogen in both species. Microplastics exhibited contrasting root responses between the two species. In L. perenne, microplastics increased root tip number and root tissue density but decreased specific root length and specific root area, suggesting a conservative root strategy. In M. sativa, microplastics reduced root length, root surface area, and fine root growth, while increasing specific root length as a compensatory response. Earthworms promoted root development, especially in L. perenne, by enhancing root length, surface area, root tips, and fine root traits. Moreover, microplastics reduced photosynthetic performance and plant growth performance, whereas earthworms enhanced them. Principal component analyses identified plant species as the primary driver of growth variation, followed by earthworms and microplastics. Redundancy analysis revealed that root length, root tissue density, fine root length, and soil NO3−–N explained 33.00%, 12.52%, 15.71%, and 24.25% of the variation in plant performance, respectively. Overall, earthworms mitigated microplastic-induced stress by improving soil nutrient availability and root development, whereas microplastic effects depended on species-specific root functional strategies.
